title: Bangladesh Measles Death Toll Crosses 1,050 in Deadliest Outbreak in Decades
excerpt: Five more children died in the past 24 hours as the outbreak — driven by Covid-era vaccination gaps and an underestimated target population — becomes Bangladesh's worst since 2005.
body:
• Bangladesh's measles death toll has reached 1,053, with five more children dying in the previous 24 hours, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
  • Since March 15, the country has recorded 175,198 suspected cases and 20,282 lab-confirmed infections, with 100 confirmed deaths and hundreds more suspected — the vast majority among unvaccinated children under two.
  • It is the deadliest measles outbreak Bangladesh has seen since 2005, driven by Covid-era immunization gaps, delayed catch-up campaigns, and a target population that authorities later admitted was underestimated.
  • An emergency campaign claims 1.97 crore children vaccinated, but cases resurged in August after a June-July dip. Health authorities are preparing a new drive targeting 16 lakh more children with 25 lakh UNICEF vaccines in the pipeline.

The toll keeps rising

Bangladesh's measles crisis deepened this week as the death toll reached 1,053, with five more children dying of measles or measles-like symptoms in a single 24-hour period, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) reported. In the same window, 1,239 new suspected cases were reported across the country.

Between March 15 and September 16, the DGHS recorded at least 175,198 suspected cases, 20,282 laboratory-confirmed infections, and 1,044 confirmed and suspected deaths, according to figures cited by Scientific American — with the toll climbing further in the days since. The majority of infections have struck unvaccinated children younger than two. Experts say the official numbers are likely an underestimate, particularly in rural areas that have struggled to obtain resources and vaccines.

The outbreak is the deadliest the South Asian country has seen since 2005. At least 1.49 lakh of those affected have required hospitalization.

How the safety net failed

Bangladesh's immunization program was once regarded as a major success story among developing nations, built on government leadership, NGO participation, and community mobilization. The current crisis shows how accumulated weaknesses undid it.

"Covid-19 disrupted routine immunisation. Some children were never brought back into the system," The Daily Star reported, citing DGHS data. A planned 2024 catch-up vaccination campaign was delayed by political unrest, and a follow-up drive in 2025 was pushed back further by strikes and continued instability, leaving large numbers of children without protection. Hard-to-reach populations — urban slum residents, migrants, and other marginalized communities — were inadequately covered, and routine follow-up to identify zero-dose children was insufficient.

Authorities responded with a large-scale emergency vaccination campaign that began April 5, targeting 18,015,064 children between six months and five years old, and reported inoculating nearly 1.97 crore children — a figure officials called 103% of target. But questions later emerged over the accuracy of population estimates after a subsequent vitamin A campaign reached around 2.26 crore children in the same age group — meaning roughly 46 lakh children had been outside the measles campaign's target. A public health vaccinologist told The Business Standard the campaign's actual coverage was closer to 81%, not 100%. Cases dipped in June and July, then resurged in August.

"These viruses are not merciful"

In a Dhaka hospital, eight-month-old Rojatun Jannat Ramisa struggled to breathe as her parents sat helplessly beside her. Her mother, Ranu Akhter, traveled hundreds of kilometers after doctors in eastern Bangladesh referred the girl to a specialized child hospital in the capital.

"Fourteen days ago, when we were at the district hospital, there were other children being treated alongside my daughter. I saw that those children also had red rashes on their bodies, sores in their mouths and fevers. It made me realize how widespread the measles outbreak is."

— Ranu Akhter, mother of a hospitalized infant, to The Associated Press

Measles causes a blotchy rash and flu-like symptoms but can develop into severe, life-threatening illness, including pneumonia and brain swelling. "These viruses are not merciful," said Sakil Faizullah, a health communications researcher at Texas A&M University and a former communications specialist at UNICEF Bangladesh. "If there is a break in the regular vaccination process, they will just attack, and that is what happened in Bangladesh."

A preventable catastrophe

Health experts caution that distinctions remain between confirmed and suspected infections and fatalities — of the deaths reported in one DGHS update, 100 were lab-confirmed and 944 were suspected cases. But the essential fact is that children are dying in extraordinary numbers from a disease that is highly preventable by vaccination.

Ninety-two percent of measles deaths have occurred among unvaccinated children, and health officials say there have been no deaths among children who received the vaccine. The ministry is preparing a new vaccination program with an initial target of 16 lakh children missed by earlier drives, and expects 25 lakh vaccines from UNICEF within two to three weeks, with vaccines worth around Tk41 crore already in the pipeline.

What comes next

Public health specialists say the campaign must be extended beyond the under-five age group — measles cases are appearing in children older than five, and experts recommend vaccinating at least all children under 10, if not 15. The Daily Star's reporting called for a thorough investigation into the governance failures that allowed the outbreak to escalate, and renewed efforts to identify and vaccinate zero-dose children in marginalized communities.

For India and the wider region, the outbreak is a warning: immunization gaps built up quietly over several years before manifesting in a single devastating year. Rebuilding confidence in the immunization system — and reaching the children every campaign misses — will determine whether the toll stops climbing.

nri_angle: Bangladesh's deadliest measles outbreak in decades is a cautionary tale for the region, including India, on how accumulated immunization gaps turn into catastrophe.
